summary: Presents RACK-TLP, a loss detection algorithm for TCP. RACK uses transmit timestamps and selective acknowledgments to start fast recovery quickly, and Tail Loss Probe (TLP) sends a probe packet to trigger recovery when losses happen at the end of a transfer.

eli5.summary: TCP needs to notice quickly when data goes missing. This method times each packet and, if the last ones seem lost, sends a nudge to find out.

questions: how does tcp detect packet loss
what is a tail loss probe
what is the rack reordering window
subtitle: A time-based way for TCP to notice lost segments quickly, plus a probe that avoids slow timeouts.

tldr.problem: Classic TCP loss detection counts duplicate ACKs (default threshold 3), which fails for short flows, lost retransmissions and reordering, so the sender falls back to a slow retransmission timeout.
tldr.mechanism: RACK records when each segment was last sent and treats a segment as lost once a later-sent segment has been delivered and a reordering window has passed. TLP sends one probe segment after about two round trips to trigger the ACK feedback RACK needs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8985 is a Standards Track document that is RECOMMENDED as an alternative to DupAck counting. It detects tail losses, lost retransmissions and reordering more efficiently, but needs per-segment transmit timestamps.

today: RFC 8985 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2021. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not replace TCP congestion control; it supplies the loss detection that feeds it.

sections.title: What RACK-TLP Is
sections.content:
RFC 8985 presents RACK-TLP, a TCP loss detection algorithm that improves on the widely implemented duplicate acknowledgment (DupAck) counting approach of RFC 5681 and RFC 6675. It is RECOMMENDED as an alternative to that earlier approach.

It has two parts. Recent Acknowledgment (RACK) detects losses quickly using time-based inferences from ACK feedback. Tail Loss Probe (TLP) quickly sends a probe segment to trigger ACK feedback, so the sender avoids a retransmission timeout (RTO).
sections.eli5: TCP needs to know when data went missing. RACK is a clever way to guess from timing, and TLP is a little nudge that makes the other side reply.

sections.title: Why DupAck Counting Falls Short
sections.content:
With traditional recovery, a sender starts fast recovery when the number of DupAcks reaches DupThresh, which defaults to 3. If that fails, it resorts to RTO recovery: the RTO is conservatively the smoothed RTT plus four times the RTT variation, lower bounded to 1 second, and the congestion window resets to the loss window (by default 1 full-sized segment).

The RFC lists three situations that needlessly push a sender into RTO recovery:

  • Tail drops. If only the last segment in a flight of 100 is lost, no DupAck arrives, the RTO expires and the window drops to 1. A loss anywhere from the first to the 97th segment would only halve the window.
  • Lost retransmissions. DupAck counting does not detect them, and slow start after the RTO can cause burst losses again.
  • Reordering. Link-layer protocols, link bonding or ECMP load balancing can deliver segments out of order. If the reordering degree exceeds DupThresh, DupAck counting causes spurious fast recovery and an unnecessary window reduction.
sections.eli5: The old way waits until three later letters show up before worrying. If the lost letter was the last one, nothing ever shows up, so you wait a very long time and then start over slowly.

sections.title: RACK and TLP: The Two Ideas
sections.content:
The two design principles are to detect losses via ACK events as much as possible, so repair happens on round-trip timescales, and to gently probe the network to solicit more ACK feedback, so the RTO never expires.

RACK rests on this rationale: if a segment is delivered out of order, the segments sent chronologically before it were either lost or reordered. Its key innovation is using per-segment transmission timestamps and SACK options instead of counting ACKs. Because it does not depend on flight size, it works for application-limited traffic. The same logic covers retransmissions, so lost retransmissions are detected too.

TLP handles sparse ACKs. After the last segment is sent, TLP sends the next new segment, or retransmits the highest-sequenced segment, in two round trips. If the probe arrives, its ACK lets RACK detect the earlier losses and start fast recovery. In the RFC's example of 100 segments where the last three are lost, recovery takes four RTTs with only a partial window reduction, instead of three RTTs plus one RTO and a reset window. If the probe is also lost, RTO recovery still applies.
sections.eli5: RACK says: a letter is lost if a letter mailed after it arrived and you have waited long enough. TLP says: if it has been quiet too long, mail one more copy of the last letter to make the other side answer.

sections.title: The Reordering Window
sections.content:
A sender cannot tell right away whether a SACK means reordering or loss, so it must wait a reordering window. RACK-TLP considers a segment S lost when both are true: a segment sent later than S has been delivered, and S has not been delivered after the estimated round-trip time plus the reordering window.

The window adapts under these rules:

  • It SHOULD be zero if no reordering has been seen and either three segments have been SACKed since the last recovery or the sender is already in fast or RTO recovery. Otherwise it starts as a small fraction of the RTT.
  • It SHOULD grow when the sender receives a DSACK option, which signals a spurious retransmission.
  • It MUST be bounded, and the bound SHOULD be SRTT.

In the detailed algorithm, the window starts at RACK.min_RTT/4. After N round trips in which a DSACK is received it becomes (N+1) * min_RTT / 4, capped at SRTT. The inflated value persists for up to 16 loss recoveries before resetting. Reordering is detected when a never-retransmitted segment below the highest acknowledged sequence (RACK.fack) is acknowledged.
sections.eli5: Sometimes letters arrive in the wrong order, so you wait a little before calling one lost. If you called one lost and it turns up twice, you learn to wait a bit longer next time.

sections.title: How a Sender Runs RACK and TLP
sections.content:
On every transmission or retransmission the sender stores the time in Segment.xmit_ts and clears Segment.lost. On each ACK it updates the minimum RTT, finds the most recently sent segment that has been delivered (RACK.segment), detects reordering, updates the reordering window and then detects losses. Segments that were retransmitted are ignored for RTT samples if the timestamp echo shows the ACK was not for the last retransmission, or if they were last retransmitted less than RACK.min_rtt ago.

A segment is marked lost when a later-sent segment has been delivered and Segment.xmit_ts + RACK.rtt + RACK.reo_wnd - Now() is zero or less. The sender SHOULD install a reordering timer so this happens on time even if no more ACKs arrive. On RTO expiration, RACK marks only the first outstanding segment as lost, plus any others older than the recent RTT plus reordering window, which cuts spurious retransmissions.

For TLP, the sender SHOULD schedule a probe timeout (PTO) after sending new data or receiving an ACK for new data, unless it is in recovery or segments have been SACKed. The PTO defaults to 2*SRTT, is 1 second when there is no SRTT, may be inflated by TLP.max_ack_delay when the flight is one segment, and is capped at the time the RTO would fire. A probe is sent only if no earlier probe is in flight and a new RTT sample has been taken. The sender SHOULD send unsent data if available, otherwise retransmit the highest-sequence segment, and it MUST then re-arm the RTO timer so RTO remains the last resort.
sections.eli5: The sender writes down when it sent each segment. When a reply comes back it checks the notes: anything sent earlier than a segment that arrived, and waited on long enough, gets sent again.

sections.title: Requirements and Probe Recovery Detection
sections.content:
RACK-TLP has these requirements. The connection MUST use SACK and the sender MUST keep SACK scoreboard information. The sender MUST store each segment's most recent transmission time with a timestamp finer than 1/4 of the connection's minimum RTT. DSACK-based window adaptation is RECOMMENDED but not required. TLP requires RACK.

A TLP retransmission that repairs the only lost segment looks like a normal cumulative ACK, which would hide the loss from congestion control. So after a TLP retransmission the sender looks for a duplicate ACK or a DSACK showing both copies arrived, meaning there was no loss. If it sees no such sign, it MUST assume a loss for congestion control purposes and SHOULD invoke a response equivalent to fast recovery.
sections.eli5: The sender must keep good notes with a clock that ticks fast enough. And if the extra copy fixed everything quietly, the sender should still admit something got lost and slow down a bit, unless the other side says both copies arrived.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The biggest advantage is that every segment, original or retransmitted, can be used to detect losses of segments sent before it. It also works with TCP Segmentation Offload because segments in one aggregate share a timestamp. The main drawback is extra state: implementations that do not already record transmission times need per-packet state expected to be either 4 or 8 octets per segment or TSO aggregate. The reordering timer can also fire early and cause spurious retransmissions, especially without DSACK.

RACK-TLP only detects losses and does not change congestion control. A segment marked lost MUST NOT be retransmitted until congestion control allows it. Proportional Rate Reduction (RFC 6937) is RECOMMENDED for the response; without it, a detected lost retransmission MUST trigger an additional congestion response. The loss recovery algorithm of RFC 6675 MUST NOT be used with RACK-TLP. The only exception to decoupling is that one outstanding loss probe may be sent even when the congestion window is full.

The RFC's worked example has a congestion window of 20 and 10 lost segments: without RACK-TLP recovery takes RTO + 4*RTT, with it 6*RTT.
sections.eli5: The new way needs more note-taking, but it catches more kinds of lost letters. It only finds the lost ones; a separate rule still decides how fast to resend.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RACK-TLP relies on information in SACK options, so its security considerations are similar to those of RFC 6675. The RFC argues that it has a lower risk profile because it is not vulnerable to ACK-splitting attacks, where a receiver or attacker sends MSS ACKs that each acknowledge one more byte. Every byte of a segment shares one transmission timestamp, so RACK.xmit_ts does not advance and the sender is not fooled.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A trickster cannot fool the sender by confirming a letter one tiny piece at a time, because the sender only cares about when the whole letter was mailed.

messages.note: The TLP timer fires 2 RTTs after the ACK.
